name: Cacoxenite
physical: Crystal healers link it to an uplifted, energetic mood
Many people keep it nearby for a lively boost
summary: Cacoxenite is a golden-brown iron phosphate whose silky sprays glow inside amethyst and quartz, prized in crystal lore for spiritual light and amplification.
intro: Cacoxenite is the golden thread inside some of the world's most prized amethysts. This iron-aluminum phosphate forms radiating sprays and fuzzy tufts of fine, silky fibers in shades of yellow, gold, orange and brown. When it is trapped within clear quartz or amethyst, it looks like tiny fireworks, hair or golden grass suspended in glass. Fine specimens from Brazil also show bundles that look like a miniature sunburst. On its own, the mineral is soft and fragile, so it is almost always seen as an inclusion, a main ingredient of stones sold as super seven and amethyst with golden inclusions. Collectors value it for the sunny glow it brings to purple crystals.
history: Cacoxenite was described in the 1820s from material found in the Czech Republic, and its name comes from the Greek words for bad and guest, because the iron in the mineral made it a nuisance to iron smelters. In metaphysical circles, its modern fame began in the 1980s and 1990s with the discovery of gold-flecked amethyst in Minas Gerais, Brazil, and its inclusion in the stone called super seven. It was embraced by crystal healers, who gave it a reputation as a booster of spiritual energy. Few old folk traditions apply to it, as it was a rarity of mineral cabinets until recently. Other localities include Germany, France and some US states, though the best crystal inclusions come from Brazil.
meaning: Crystal practitioners regard cacoxenite as a stone of golden spiritual light. Inside amethyst or quartz, it is said to amplify the host's vibration, adding a sunny, uplifting character to the calm of violet. Associated with the Crown, Third Eye and sometimes the Solar Plexus, it is used by those who want to bring more joy and energy into meditation. Many describe a feeling of warmth or spark, as if a window has been opened. It is also linked to spiritual awakening and transformation, and people may turn to it during periods of change. It is usually appreciated as an accent within another stone, and its value is as much in the way it enhances other crystals.
howToUse: Look for cacoxenite as inclusions in amethyst or quartz points and hold such a crystal in meditation, resting it at the Third Eye or the crown of the head. Gaze at the golden sprays in soft light, letting your mind relax into the patterns. Keep a piece on your altar as a symbol of light within calm. Wear a small cabochon or tumbled stone as a pendant for a gentle uplift. In a grid, pair it with amethyst, clear quartz and selenite. Because it is delicate on its own, handle collector specimens carefully and display them out of reach of children and pets.
care: Pure cacoxenite is soft, at 3 to 4 on the Mohs scale, and can be porous, so avoid soaking it. If it is included in quartz or amethyst, the host stone will be hardier, but the inclusion still deserves care. Clean with a dry soft brush or cloth, with no water or chemicals. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight, and avoid strong sun if the host is amethyst, which can fade. Store in a padded box and keep away from hard stones that could scratch it.
identify: Cacoxenite appears as golden, brown, yellow or orange radiating sprays, tufts or hair-like fibers, usually inside clear or purple quartz. Under magnification the fibers are fine and silky and radiate outward from a point. Look-alikes include goethite, limonite and rutile, which can also form golden needles; rutile needles tend to be straighter and more metallic. Dyed or glass-based fakes have regular, repeated patterns. Super seven stones often contain cacoxenite along with other minerals, so ask for details if you want to be sure.

faq.a: Cacoxenite is a golden-yellow to brown iron aluminum phosphate that forms silky, radiating sprays. It is seen most often as an inclusion inside amethyst and quartz, and is a key ingredient in stones sold as super seven.
People use it for spiritual uplift, amplification of other crystals and meditation. It is linked to the Crown and Third Eye chakras and valued for adding a golden, energizing note to calm amethyst.
It is best to avoid it. Pure cacoxenite is soft and porous, so water can harm it. If it is within quartz, the host is waterproof, but it is safer to cleanse with smoke, sound or a dry soft brush.
